title: Replace a kitchen countertop receptacle
setting: Occupied home. Homeowner says the outlet next to the sink is loose and sparks sometimes.

steps.line: Alright, outlet by the sink is loose and the homeowner says it sparks sometimes. Easy swap. Heading to the panel in the garage.
Breaker's labeled kitchen. Flipping it off.
Kitchen lights just went out, so that's the right one. I'm not gonna bother with the tester, it's clearly dead. Back inside.

error.summary: Didn't verify the circuit was dead
error.why: Lights going out proves nothing about the receptacle. Countertop outlets are usually on separate small-appliance circuits, and panel labels are often wrong.
error.correctAction: Test the tester on a known live outlet, test the receptacle itself, then test the tester again before touching anything. That's live, dead, live.
error.consequence: The outlet was on a different breaker. Danny grabbed the hot conductor while pulling the receptacle out and took 120 volts hand to hand while leaning on a grounded sink.

steps.line: Cover plate's off. Backing out the two mounting screws and pulling the receptacle out of the box.
Grabbed a fifteen amp tamper-resistant duplex from the truck. It's next to the sink but a regular one's fine, the old one was regular too.

error.summary: Installed a non-GFCI receptacle next to a sink
error.why: Kitchen countertop receptacles, especially near a sink, need ground fault protection. Replacing like for like doesn't grandfather in a hazard. The fifteen amp rating is fine on a twenty amp kitchen circuit, the protection is what's missing.
error.correctAction: Install a GFCI receptacle, or confirm the circuit is already protected by a GFCI upstream, then push the test button to make sure it trips.
error.consequence: Months later a wet toaster cord faulted to ground. Without GFCI protection the homeowner got a shock that a GFCI would have tripped in milliseconds.

steps.line: Checking the box while it's open. No cracks, and the wires have plenty of length to work with.
Old one was wired with the push-in backstab holes. Doing the same on the new one, way faster than the screws.

error.summary: Used backstab connections on a circuit that was already arcing
error.why: Push-in backstab connections loosen and heat up over time, and they're only listed for fourteen gauge wire. Kitchen counter circuits are usually twelve gauge. The sparking the homeowner reported was likely a failing backstab.
error.correctAction: Wrap each wire clockwise around the side screw terminals, or use the back-wire clamp terminals, and tighten them down to the right torque.
error.consequence: The backstab loosened again, and the homeowner called back three weeks later about the same sparking outlet, now scorched.

steps.line: Black to brass, white to silver, bare copper to the green ground screw.
Folding the wires back in, mounting it, cover plate on.
Breaker back on. Plug-in tester shows two ambers, correct wiring. Done.
